tldr: By leveraging the geometric structure of visual plans (trajectories and bounding boxes) and generating entire primitives in a single pass with a lightweight drafter, this study achieves far faster inference speeds and higher spatial accuracy than autoregressive VLMs.
hero_caption: Overall overview of VFlash. Taking advantage of the predetermined structure of visual primitives (2D/3D trajectories and point cloud motion), it generates entire blocks in parallel within a single forward pass. It cuts latency by roughly 80% on edge devices like the Jetson Thor while achieving higher trajectory prediction accuracy than autoregressive (AR) decoding.
overview:
In physical AI domains like robotics and autonomous driving, vision-language models (VLMs) are expected to serve as high-level brains. Rather than operating purely in language, these models guide actions by outputting "visual plans" such as target locations and motion trajectories. However, conventional autoregressive (AR) VLMs generate coordinates one token at a time. As trajectories grow longer or 3D coordinates are added, the number of generation steps explodes, creating a major obstacle to meeting the real-time requirements of physical robot control loops.

To solve this, the authors observed that the data structure of visual primitives (such as trajectories and boxes) is known in advance. Once the number of trajectory points and their dimensionality (2D or 3D) are specified, the layout of the token sequence to be generated is fixed. Leveraging this property, they propose "VFlash," a method that uses a lightweight diffusion drafter to generate entire primitives in parallel in a single forward pass. Unlike conventional speculative decoding, VFlash does not demand exact token-level agreement with the target VLM; instead, it directly accepts syntactically valid geometric predictions, representing a breakthrough approach.

Evaluated on benchmarks across robot manipulation (MolmoSpaces, LIBERO) and autonomous driving (NAVSIM, Waymo), VFlash reduced inference latency by approximately 80% compared to standard AR generation. Even more surprisingly, spatial error was lower than when coordinates were generated autoregressively one by one, improving prediction accuracy itself. It also demonstrated significantly higher task success rates over conventional baselines in downstream robot manipulation tasks.
contributions: Proposed Flash Primitive Decoding (FPD), which leverages the known layout structure of visual primitives to predict entire variable-length trajectories and boxes in parallel in a single pass.

Removed the strict exact token-agreement constraint of conventional speculative decoding, demonstrating that directly accepting structurally valid geometric outputs allows a lightweight drafter to exceed the target VLM in spatial accuracy.

Evaluated across diverse tasks including robot manipulation, autonomous driving, and dense 3D point cloud forecasting, achieving an approximately 25x speedup in 3D point motion forecasting and roughly an 80% latency reduction on edge hardware for physical robots (Jetson Thor).
Conditioned action models (such as World Action Models) on visual plans generated by VFlash, significantly boosting the average task success rate on MolmoSpaces from 62.6% to 70.2%.

sections.heading: Why solve coordinates one by one autoregressively?
sections.summary: In visual planning for robotics, sequential token generation by autoregressive VLMs acts as a latency bottleneck. VFlash exploits the structure of geometric primitives to generate them all at once, achieving both major speedups and higher accuracy.
sections.details:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are becoming central to high-level planning in physical AI fields such as robotics and autonomous driving. Beyond reasoning in natural language, VLMs can generate "visual plans"—such as bounding boxes and 2D/3D trajectories—to explicitly specify where to focus in the environment and how to move next.

However, existing autoregressive (AR) VLMs suffer from a structural weakness. Because they generate trajectory coordinate tokens sequentially one by one, the required generation steps increase dramatically as trajectories become longer or when combining 2D image coordinates with 3D real-world coordinates. When a robot needs to frequently update its plan in response to environmental changes, the latency caused by this sequential decoding becomes a critical constraint.

While speculative decoding (where a draft model proposes candidates and the target model verifies them in parallel) has gained attention for acceleration, conventional methods are designed to guarantee exact agreement with the target model's output token sequence. However, the authors point out that in visual planning, "faithfully reproducing the target model's token sequence" and "producing a geometrically accurate plan" are two entirely different things.

Once a visual primitive's format (box or trajectory) and point count are specified, its overall layout is known in advance. VFlash exploits this structure by using a lightweight drafter model to jointly predict the entire primitive, accepting syntactically valid predictions directly without token-agreement verification. This enables extremely fast, high-accuracy visual planning akin to human reflexive, intuitive thinking (System-1).

sections.heading: Joint generation leveraging geometry: Flash Primitive Decoding
sections.summary: VFlash determines primitive specifications via tool calling and predicts entire blocks in parallel within a single pass using a lightweight diffusion drafter. It adopts a hybrid setup: verified speculative decoding for text, and direct acceptance based on structural validity for visual primitives.
sections.details:
Here, we explain the core decoding technique of VFlash, "Flash Primitive Decoding (FPD)," and its underlying design principles.

### 2.1 Limitations and Insights from Speculative Decoding
The baseline DFlash uses a lightweight block diffusion drafter conditioned on target VLM features to guess $\gamma$ tokens in a single pass. However, under standard verification, if even the very first token deviates from the target model's greedy output, all subsequent tokens are discarded. While exact contextual matching is essential for text, in trajectory coordinates, a deviation of just one bin (a tiny numerical difference) triggers rejection, eroding the benefits of acceleration.

### 2.2 How Flash Primitive Decoding (FPD) Works
In VFlash, the type, dimensionality, and number of points of the primitive to be generated are declared in advance via tool calling. For example, if declared as a "10-point 2D+3D trajectory," the entire block length $B(s)$ and the role of each token (axis coordinate, delimiter, etc.) are completely fixed. This allows the drafter to predict all coordinates in parallel (conditional independent prediction) in a single forward pass.

### 2.3 Token Representation and Alignment
To stably generate long, variable-length primitives in parallel, two principles are introduced. The first is "boundary alignment," which treats an entire primitive as a single draft block rather than chunking it into fixed-width windows. The second is "positional alignment," which pre-assigns the semantic role of each slot (point index, axis, delimiter). For coordinate representation, it supports both dedicated special tokens discretized into 0–1,000 bins and text-numeric formats using signed 5-digit fixed-width grids.

### 2.4 Training Method
With the target VLM weights frozen, the drafter—a shallow 5-layer non-causal (bidirectional) transformer—is trained. Crucially, it is trained using cross-entropy loss against annotated ground-truth coordinates, not the target VLM's outputs. In other words, rather than mimicking the target's behavior, the drafter is directly optimized to predict the ground-truth geometry.

### 2.5 Inference Acceptance Rules
At inference time, normal text is generated using verified DFlash with 16 tokens at a time. When a primitive start token appears, the system switches to FPD mode and drafts a block of the specified length all at once. As long as the generated coordinates satisfy vocabulary and formatting constraints, they are accepted directly without verifying token agreement with the target model. Afterward, the target model performs a single forward pass to update its KV cache and extract features to pass to downstream models.

sections.heading: Not just fast: experimental results outperform the autoregressive model
sections.summary: Evaluated across 2D/3D trajectory forecasting, bounding box detection, point cloud prediction, and downstream robot manipulation and autonomous driving tasks. VFlash not only cuts latency dramatically, but also achieves higher spatial accuracy than the autoregressive target model.
sections.details:
The performance of VFlash was validated across three perspectives: visual primitive prediction accuracy, effectiveness in downstream tasks, and inference speed.

### 3.1 Prediction Performance of Visual Primitives
- **2D Trajectory Prediction**: On ShareRobot-Bench and VABench-V, VFlash reduced all error metrics compared to the original AR target (3–6% improvements in Discrete Fréchet Distance and RMSE). On VABench-V, it achieved roughly 40% error reduction over the prior best model (LoHo-Manip).
- **2D Bounding Boxes**: On COCO and Dense200, incorporating an AR fallback mechanism for low-confidence cases maintained an average F1 score on par with AR while achieving a 2.6–2.8x speedup.
- **3D Trajectory Prediction**: Evaluated across InternA1, AgiBot, and MolmoBot, Average Displacement Error (ADE) dropped by 18–61% relative to the AR target. In particular, on AgiBot, the proportion of predictions falling within a 5 cm error margin improved dramatically from 40% (AR) to 74% (VFlash) in the joint 2D+3D output setting. While AR accuracy degraded when jointly predicting 2D and 3D coordinates, VFlash preserved high accuracy by solving them in parallel.
- **Dense 3D Point Motion Forecasting**: Evaluated on PointMotionBench with MolmoMotion-AR as the base, VFlash reduced ADE by 27% and FDE (Final Displacement Error) by 19% on the DAVIS dataset, while boosting generation speed by approximately 25x.

### 3.2 Downstream Task Applications (Robotics & Autonomous Driving)
- **MolmoSpaces (Robot Manipulation)**: Feeding VFlash-generated 2D+3D trajectory features into a Cosmos-based World Action Model (WAM) raised the overall task average success rate from 62.6% (baseline) to 70.2%. This is significantly higher than using AR-generated trajectories (61.0%), showing that high-precision plans from VFlash strongly support action generation.
- **LIBERO Family**: On LIBERO-PRO, which evaluates robustness to disturbances, the success rate improved by 6.8 percentage points compared to language instructions alone, showing pronounced gains in tasks requiring spatial reasoning.
- **Autonomous Driving**: On NAVSIM and Waymo, fine-tuning a small action head conditioned on VFlash plans with reinforcement learning achieved 90.7 PDMS on NAVSIM and 7.86 RFS on Waymo, matching state-of-the-art performance.

### 3.3 Throughput and Latency Analysis
Measurements were conducted on the Jetson Thor embedded robotics board, desktop-class DGX Spark, and server-grade H100. In MolmoSpaces on Jetson Thor, decoding time accounted for 75–87% of the total step time under standard AR decoding; VFlash sped up this decoding time by 12–42x, slashing total pipeline latency by roughly 80% (over 5.1x throughput). Furthermore, when token count increased from 36 to 84, decoding time remained flat at 72–78 ms, confirming the distinct advantage of parallel generation where latency does not grow with more detailed plans.

sections.heading: How it differs from prior work: freeing visual plans from the curse of exact matching
sections.summary: This section organizes prior work in speculative decoding and efficiency for physical AI, highlighting VFlash's uniqueness. Instead of pursuing exact token agreement, it leverages geometric structure to balance spatial accuracy and speed.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of embodied VLMs, parallel/speculative decoding, and System-1 fast-decision models.

### Embodied VLMs and Visual Planning
Using VLMs to generate bounding boxes or trajectories as conditioning inputs for downstream policies has been actively explored. However, past research focused on "what to predict" without sufficiently addressing the latency challenge of "how to generate them quickly." In AR generation solving one coordinate at a time, latency accumulates with every additional waypoint.

### Differences from Speculative Decoding
Techniques such as Medusa, EAGLE, and DFlash have been developed for accelerating language models. Spec-VLA and others have also been proposed in robotics, but they primarily aim to "faithfully reproduce the target model's token distribution" and roll back generation upon token mismatches. In contrast, VFlash is built on the finding that for visual primitives, "direct predictions by the drafter are geometrically more accurate," completely removing the constraint of target token agreement.

### Visual Prediction as System-1 Reasoning
Recent efforts (such as Jev) attempt to realize human-like intuitive, fast thinking (System-1) in AI. VFlash brings this System-1 philosophy into the generation of complete geometric primitives, achieving both high speed and accuracy.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: VFlash leverages the structure of visual primitives to achieve fast, accurate parallel planning without relying on autoregression. It delivers an important finding: autoregressive models are not the ceiling for output quality.
sections.details:
This paper introduced VFlash, a framework that replaces sequential coordinate generation with parallel prediction by taking advantage of the known geometric structure of visual plans.

Its key finding is that "generating visual plans useful for downstream tasks does not require faithfully reproducing the token sequence of an autoregressive model." Drafts produced in a single pass by a lightweight drafter trained on ground-truth annotations actually achieved lower trajectory errors than the autoregressive target, while delivering an approximately 25x speedup in 3D point cloud forecasting.

Experiments in robot manipulation and autonomous driving also demonstrated that accelerated plans clearly boost action model performance. Future work is expected to explore whether generating multiple complementary primitives simultaneously within a fixed latency budget can further enhance control capabilities.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details, coordinate frames, and hardware profiling
sections.summary: Provides details on coordinate quantization specifications, special token definitions, drafter architecture, and TensorRT edge implementations.
sections.details:
The appendix provides numerous key details regarding reproducibility and implementation.

### Coordinate Representation and Quantization Rules
The base VLM uses dedicated numeric tokens from <0> to <1000> alongside primitive delimiter tokens. Robot 3D coordinates (XYZ) in the camera frame are linearly quantized across X=[-5, 5]m, Y=[-5, 5]m, and Z=[0, 10]m into 1,001 bins (roughly 1 cm resolution). Points projected outside the image frame are assigned an <oof> (out-of-frame) token. For text-numeric models like MolmoMotion, a fixed-width grid consisting of a sign and 5 digit slots is used, masking unused higher digits to preserve positional alignment.

### Model Configuration and Training Setup
The target VLM pairs a MoonViT-SO-400M image encoder with Qwen3-4B via an MLP. The drafter is a 5-layer transformer following the Qwen3 architecture (around 537M trainable parameters) conditioned on concatenated intermediate features from layers 1, 9, 17, 25, and 33 of the target VLM. The drafter is trained using uniformly weighted cross-entropy loss against ground-truth coordinates.

### Acceleration Implementation with TensorRT
Evaluations were conducted on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, DGX Spark, and H100. Models were compiled into TensorRT engines via ONNX and run in FP16 with FMHA (Flash Multi-Head Attention) and XQA kernels via the Edge-LLM CuTe DSL plugin. Rigorous timing benchmarks were recorded at batch size 1 in physical deployment environments, including host-side overhead.

takeaways: For tasks where the output format and length are known in advance (like visual plans with trajectories or boxes), joint parallel decoding without autoregression is vastly faster and yields higher accuracy.
In speculative decoding for multimodal geometric outputs, clinging to exact token agreement with the target VLM is unnecessary; directly accepting structurally valid outputs is far more practical.
Decoding latency is reduced by roughly 80% even on edge devices like the Jetson Thor, opening a practical path toward integrating VLMs into high-frequency robot control loops (System-1 reasoning).
limitations: The primitive format and point count must be predetermined (e.g., via tool calling), meaning it cannot be applied as-is to completely open-ended, unstructured outputs.

In text-tokenized numerical predictions such as dense 3D point cloud forecasting, while the acceleration gains are massive, there is a minor trade-off where final displacement error slightly increases on certain datasets (such as WorldTrack).
In bounding box generation, an autoregressive (AR) fallback is necessary for low-confidence cases to prevent performance drops in crowded scenes.
